claim: The controllability of our social environment has a profound impact on our behavior and mental health.
source: The controllability of our social environment has a profound impact on our behavior and mental health.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract supported by citations in the introduction to research on uncontrollable stress, pain, and learned helplessness.

claim: 48 participants performed a task where their current choices either did (Controllable), or did not (Uncontrollable), influence partners' future proposals.
source: Here, 48 participants performed a task where their current choices either did (Controllable), or did not (Uncontrollable), influence partners' future proposals.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental design in the abstract.

claim: Computational modeling revealed that people engaged a mental model of forward thinking (FT; i.e., calculating the downstream effects of current actions) to estimate social controllability in both Controllable and Uncontrollable conditions.
source: Computational modeling revealed that people engaged a mental model of forward thinking (FT; i.e., calculating the downstream effects of current actions) to estimate social controllability in both Controllable and Uncontrollable conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: A large-scale online replication study (n=1342) supported the finding that people engaged forward thinking to estimate social controllability.
source: A large-scale online replication study (n=1342) supported this finding.
evidence: This is supported by the replication study data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) computed the projected total values of current actions during forward planning.
source: Using functional magnetic resonance imaging (n=48), we further demonstrated that the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) computed the projected total values of current actions during forward planning, supporting the neural realization of the forward-thinking model.
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data showing vmPFC activation correlated with model-derived value estimates.

claim: Humans use vmPFC-dependent forward thinking to estimate and exploit social controllability.
source: These findings demonstrate that humans use vmPFC-dependent FT to estimate and exploit social controllability, expanding the role of this neurocomputational mechanism beyond spatial and cognitive contexts.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the combined behavioral, computational, and neural data.

claim: A lack of controllability has a profound impact on mental health, as demonstrated by decades of research on uncontrollable stress, pain, and learned helplessness.
source: A lack of controllability has a profound impact on mental health, as has been demonstrated by decades of research on uncontrollable stress, pain, and learned helplessness (Maier and Seligman, 1976; Maier and Watkins, 2005; Overmier, 1968; Weiss, 1968).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: High levels of controllability have been associated with better mental health outcomes such as higher subjective well-being and less negative affect.
source: Conversely, high levels of controllability have been associated with better mental health outcomes such as higher subjective well-being (Lachman and Weaver, 1998) and less negative affect (Maier and Seligman, 2016; Southwick and Southwick, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The neurocomputational mechanisms underlying social controllability have not been systematically investigated.
source: Nevertheless, despite the importance, the neurocomputational mechanisms underlying social controllability have not been systematically investigated.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in the literature that motivates the current study.

claim: People use mental models to exploit social controllability, for instance via forward simulation.
source: Based on previous work demonstrating the computational mechanisms of controllability in non-social environments, here we hypothesize that people use mental models to exploit social controllability, for instance via forward simulation.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis of the study, based on prior work in non-social contexts.

claim: In non-social contexts, controllability quantifies the extent to which the acquisition of outcomes can be influenced by the choice of actions.
source: In non-social contexts, it has been proposed that controllability quantifies the extent to which the acquisition of outcomes, and particularly desired outcomes, can be influenced by the choice of actions (Huys and Dayan, 2009; Dorfman and Gershman, 2019; Ligneul, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: Agents need to learn the association between actions and state transitions and potential outcomes in order to simulate future possibilities and make decisions.
source: In these non-social settings, agents need to learn the association between actions and state (event) transitions and potential outcomes in order to simulate future possibilities (Pezzulo et al., 2013; Szpunar et al., 2014) and make decisions (Daw et al., 2011; Dolan and Dayan, 2013; Doll et al., 2015; Gläscher et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research on decision-making.

claim: Both under- and over-estimation of controllability could be detrimental to behavior depending on the complexity of the environment.
source: It has also been hypothesized that both under- and over-estimation of controllability could be detrimental to behavior (Huys and Dayan, 2009) depending on the complexity of the environment.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior theoretical work.

claim: It remains unknown whether both under- and over-estimation of controllability is detrimental for social controllability.
source: Yet, it remains unknown whether this is true for social controllability.
evidence: This is a statement about a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: People can learn the influence of their own actions on others during an iterative inspection game.
source: For example, Hampton et al., 2008 showed that people can learn the influence of their own actions on others during an iterative inspection game; and that the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) tracked expected reward given the degree of expected influence (Hampton et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) tracked expected reward given the degree of expected influence during an iterative inspection game.
source: For example, Hampton et al., 2008 showed that people can learn the influence of their own actions on others during an iterative inspection game; and that the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) tracked expected reward given the degree of expected influence (Hampton et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Individuals differ drastically in their ability to manage their social images and exert influence on others during bargaining.
source: In other types of strategic games such as bargaining, it has been suggested that individuals differ drastically in their ability to manage their social images and exert influence on others, a behavioral phenomenon subserved by underlying neural differences in prefrontal regions (Bhatt et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Humans are able to use forward planning and mentally simulate future interactions in an iterative trust game.
source: Furthermore, through the application of an interactive partially observable Markov decision process model, Hula et al., 2015 found that humans are able to use forward planning and mentally simulate future interactions in an iterative trust game (Hula et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Learning the structure of the social environment is crucial for exerting influence.
source: All of these studies suggest that learning the structure of the social environment is crucial for exerting influence, yet none have systematically examined the computational underpinnings of social controllability in a group setting where an agent plays with multiple other players that constitute a more social-like environment.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from prior studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: No prior studies have systematically examined the computational underpinnings of social controllability in a group setting where an agent plays with multiple other players.
source: All of these studies suggest that learning the structure of the social environment is crucial for exerting influence, yet none have systematically examined the computational underpinnings of social controllability in a group setting where an agent plays with multiple other players that constitute a more social-like environment.
evidence: This is a statement about a gap in the literature.

claim: The ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) has been shown to signal expected values across a wide range of settings.
source: Neurally, along with recent findings about its role in providing a representational substrate for cognitive tasks (Behrens et al., 2018; Niv, 2019; Schuck et al., 2016), the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) has been shown to signal expected values across a wide range of settings (Boorman et al., 2009; Kable and Glimcher, 2007; FitzGerald et al., 2009; Behrens et al., 2008; Bartra et al., 2013; Venkatraman et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The vmPFC provides a representational substrate for cognitive tasks.
source: Neurally, along with recent findings about its role in providing a representational substrate for cognitive tasks (Behrens et al., 2018; Niv, 2019; Schuck et al., 2016), the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) has been shown to signal expected values across a wide range of settings (Boorman et al., 2009; Kable and Glimcher, 2007; FitzGerald et al., 2009; Behrens et al., 2008; Bartra et al., 2013; Venkatraman et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The majority of studies have focused on the role of the vmPFC in encoding the subjective values of non-social choices.
source: The majority of studies have focused on the role of the vmPFC in encoding the subjective values of non-social choices (Boorman et al., 2009; FitzGerald et al., 2009; Kable and Glimcher, 2007; Venkatraman et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a statement about the focus of prior research, supported by citations.

claim: Accumulating evidence pinpoints to a central role of the vmPFC in computing the value of social choices.
source: Nevertheless, accumulating evidence also pinpoints to a central role of the vmPFC in computing the value of social choices (Behrens et al., 2008; Hampton et al., 2008; Hiser and Koenigs, 2018), such as expected values computed based on learned influence (Hampton et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Both social and non-social subjective values reliably activate the vmPFC.
source: A recent meta-analysis suggests that both social and non-social subjective values reliably activate the vmPFC (Bartra et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a meta-analysis.

claim: The vmPFC will play an important role in social controllability where the value of future events should be simulated and computed.
source: Thus, we expect that the vmPFC will also play an important role in social controllability where the value of future events should be simulated and computed.
evidence: This is a prediction based on prior research on the vmPFC.

claim: Humans exploit social controllability by implementing forward thinking (FT) and mentally simulating future interactions.
source: In the current study, we hypothesize that humans exploit social controllability by implementing forward thinking (FT) and mentally simulating future interactions.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis of the study.

claim: Social agents will use forward planning to take into account not only decision variables related to the present interaction with a current partner, but also those related to future interactions with other partners from the same milieu.
source: In particular, we consider the long-lasting effect that one's current interaction with one other person can have on future interactions with many others who constitute the social environment, for instance by developing a reputation. We predict that social agents will use forward planning to take into account not only decision variables related to the present interaction with a current partner, but also those related to future interactions with other partners from the same milieu.
evidence: This is a prediction of the study.

claim: The choice values integrating the planned paths would be signaled in the vmPFC.
source: Finally, we hypothesize that the choice values integrating the planned paths would be signaled in the vmPFC.
evidence: This is a hypothesis of the study.

claim: Both in-person and online participants completed an economic exchange task where they did (Controllable) or did not (Uncontrollable) influence their partners' proposals of monetary offers in the future.
source: Both in-person and online participants completed an economic exchange task where they did (Controllable) or did not (Uncontrollable) influence their partners' proposals of monetary offers in the future (see Figure 1a and b, and Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Participants were told that they were playing members coming from two different teams, one each for the two controllability conditions.
source: Participants were told that they were playing members coming from two different teams, one each for the two controllability conditions (in a counterbalanced order across subjects); in fact, they played with a computer algorithm in both cases.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Participants played with a computer algorithm in both conditions.
source: Participants were told that they were playing members coming from two different teams, one each for the two controllability conditions (in a counterbalanced order across subjects); in fact, they played with a computer algorithm in both cases.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Participants played against each team as the responder in a social exchange game adapted from the ultimatum game.
source: Participants played against each team as the responder in a social exchange game adapted from the ultimatum game (Camerer, 2011) (single-shot games with 40 different partners (rounds) per team for the fMRI sample, and 30 rounds for the online sample).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: In the Uncontrollable condition, participants' current choices had no influence on the next offers from their partners.
source: In the Uncontrollable condition, on each round, participants were offered a split of $20 from their partners and asked to decide whether to accept or reject the offer. Unbeknownst to participants, the actual offer was randomly drawn from a normal distribution (rounded and restricted to be between $2 and $8 (inclusive) for the fMRI sample and between $1 and $9 (inclusive) for the online sample; the first offer was always $5). Here, participants' current choices had no influence on the next offers from their partners.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: In the Controllable condition, participants could exert control over their partners using their own actions.
source: The Controllable condition was the same except that participants could exert control over their partners using their own actions.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: In the Controllable condition, partners increased the next offer by $0, $1, or $2 (probability of ⅓ each) if the participant rejected the present offer.
source: Specifically, participants' current decisions (i.e., to accept or reject the offer) influenced the next offers from their partners in a systematic manner. Subject only to being between $1 and $9 (inclusive), partners increased the next offer by $0, $1, or $2 (probability of ⅓ each, subject to the constraints) if the participant rejected the present offer, and decreased the next offers by $0, $1, or $2 (probability of ⅓ each, again subject to the constraints) if the participant accepted the current offer (Figure 1b and Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: In the Controllable condition, partners decreased the next offers by $0, $1, or $2 (probability of ⅓ each) if the participant accepted the current offer.
source: Specifically, participants' current decisions (i.e., to accept or reject the offer) influenced the next offers from their partners in a systematic manner. Subject only to being between $1 and $9 (inclusive), partners increased the next offer by $0, $1, or $2 (probability of ⅓ each, subject to the constraints) if the participant rejected the present offer, and decreased the next offers by $0, $1, or $2 (probability of ⅓ each, again subject to the constraints) if the participant accepted the current offer (Figure 1b and Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: At the end of the task, participants rated how much control they believed they had over their partners' offers in each condition using a 0–100 scale.
source: At the end of the task, after all the trials were completed, we asked participants to rate how much control they believed they had over their partners' offers in each condition using a 0–100 scale to measure their perceived action-offer contingency ('self-reported/perceived controllability' hereafter).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: In the fMRI study, on 60% of the trials, participants were asked about their emotional state on a scale of 0 (unhappy) to 100 (happy) after they made a choice.
source: In the fMRI study, on 60% of the trials, participants were also asked about their emotional state (How do you feel?) on a scale of 0 (unhappy) to 100 (happy) after they made a choice (i.e., 24 ratings per condition; see Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Participants were not instructed about the statistics of the task environment nor the nature of the condition they were playing.
source: Note that participants were not instructed about the statistics of the task environment nor the nature of the condition they were playing, although the instruction about the existence of two separate teams was provided to encourage participants to learn contingent rules and norms within each condition (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: If participants were able to detect social controllability correctly within each condition, they would show strategic decisions that exert appropriate levels of control over others' subsequent choices.
source: If participants were able to detect social controllability correctly within each condition, they would show strategic decisions that exert appropriate levels of control over others' subsequent choices.
evidence: This is a prediction about what would be observed if participants detected controllability.

claim: Participants received higher offers over time under the Controllable compared to the Uncontrollable condition.
source: First, we found that despite the same starting offer of $5, participants indeed received higher offers over time under the Controllable compared to the Uncontrollable condition (meanC=5.9, meanU=4.8, t(47.45)=4.33, p<0.001; Figure 2a1, a2), indicating that individuals in general successfully exerted influence over the offers made by partners when they were given control.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the behavioral data and shown in Figure 2a1, a2.

claim: Individuals in general successfully exerted influence over the offers made by partners when they were given control.
source: First, we found that despite the same starting offer of $5, participants indeed received higher offers over time under the Controllable compared to the Uncontrollable condition (meanC=5.9, meanU=4.8, t(47.45)=4.33, p<0.001; Figure 2a1, a2), indicating that individuals in general successfully exerted influence over the offers made by partners when they were given control.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral data showing higher offers in the Controllable condition.

claim: Overall rejection rates were not different between the Controllable and Uncontrollable conditions.
source: On average, rejection rates in the two conditions were comparable (meanC=50.8%, meanU=49.1%, t(67.87)=0.43, p=0.67; Figure 2b1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the behavioral data and shown in Figure 2b1.

claim: Participants were more likely to reject medium to high ($4–9) offers in the Controllable condition.
source: By separating the trials each individual experienced into three levels of offer sizes (low: $1–3, medium: $4–6, and high: $7–9) and then aggregating across all individuals, we further examined whether rejection rates varied as a function of offer size. We found that participants were more likely to reject medium to high ($4–9) offers in the Controllable condition, while they showed comparable rejection rates for the low offers ($1–3) between the two conditions (low ($1–3): meanC=77%, meanU=87%, t(22)=–1.35, p=0.19; middle ($4–6): meanC=66%, meanU=45%, t(47)=5.41, p<0.001; high ($7–9): meanC=28%, meanU=8%, t(72.50)=4.00, p<0.001; Figure 2b2; see Figure 2—figure supplement 2 for rejection rates by each offer size).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the behavioral data and shown in Figure 2b2.

claim: Participants showed comparable rejection rates for the low offers ($1–3) between the two conditions.
source: We found that participants were more likely to reject medium to high ($4–9) offers in the Controllable condition, while they showed comparable rejection rates for the low offers ($1–3) between the two conditions (low ($1–3): meanC=77%, meanU=87%, t(22)=–1.35, p=0.19; middle ($4–6): meanC=66%, meanU=45%, t(47)=5.41, p<0.001; high ($7–9): meanC=28%, meanU=8%, t(72.50)=4.00, p<0.001; Figure 2b2; see Figure 2—figure supplement 2 for rejection rates by each offer size).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the behavioral data and shown in Figure 2b2.

claim: Participants behaved in a strategic way to utilize their influence over the partners.
source: These results suggest that participants behaved in a strategic way to utilize their influence over the partners.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the rejection patterns observed in the data.

claim: There was no significant difference in emotional rating between the Controllable and the Uncontrollable conditions.
source: One possible confound is that individuals may have experienced different affective states in the two conditions and changed their choice behaviors. However, this seemed unlikely because there was no significant difference in emotional rating between the Controllable and the Uncontrollable conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the emotional rating data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Participants reported higher self-reported controllability for the Controllable than the Uncontrollable condition.
source: Indeed, participants reported higher self-reported controllability for the Controllable than the Uncontrollable condition (meanC=65.9, meanU=43.7, t(74.55)=4.10, p<0.001; Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the self-reported controllability data and shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The mean level of self-reported controllability for the Uncontrollable condition was 43.7%, which was substantially higher than their actual level of controllability on future offers made by the partners (0%).
source: Besides the clear indication of individuals' recognition of the difference in controllability between conditions, the mean level of self-reported controllability for the Uncontrollable condition was 43.7%, which was still substantially higher than their actual level of controllability on future offers made by the partners (0%).
evidence: This is an observation from the self-reported controllability data.

claim: Participants could develop an illusory sense of control when they had no actual influence over their partners' offers.
source: This result might suggest that participants could develop an illusory sense of control when they had no actual influence over their partners' offers.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that self-reported controllability was higher than actual controllability in the Uncontrollable condition.

claim: Participants took longer time to make their decisions in the Controllable condition than the Uncontrollable condition.
source: In addition, we examined response times as an exploratory analysis and found that participants took longer time to make their decisions in the Controllable condition than the Uncontrollable condition. These results again suggest that participants differentiated the controllability between conditions (meanC=1.75±0.38, meanU=1.53±0.38; paired t-test t(47)=4.34, p<0.001; Figure 2d).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the response time data and shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Participants were able to exploit and perceive their influence in a social environment when they had influence.
source: Taken together, these findings demonstrate that participants were able to exploit and perceive their influence in a social environment when they had influence, although they have developed an illusion of control, at least to some degree, even when controllability did not exist.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the behavioral results.

claim: Participants have developed an illusion of control, at least to some degree, even when controllability did not exist.
source: Taken together, these findings demonstrate that participants were able to exploit and perceive their influence in a social environment when they had influence, although they have developed an illusion of control, at least to some degree, even when controllability did not exist.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the behavioral results.

claim: People can use future-oriented thinking and mentally simulate future scenarios when their current actions have an impact on the future.
source: Previous studies on value-based decision-making have shown that people can use future-oriented thinking and mentally simulate future scenarios when their current actions have an impact on the future (Daw et al., 2011; Gläscher et al., 2010; Lee et al., 2014; Moran et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Individuals use forward thinking to estimate the impact of their behavior on future social interactions.
source: Relying on this framework, we hypothesized that individuals use FT to estimate the impact of their behavior on future social interactions.
evidence: This is the hypothesis of the study.

claim: The forward thinking models assume that an agent computes the values of action by summing up the current value (CV) and the future value (FV) based on her estimation of the amount of controllability she has over the social interactions.
source: To test this hypothesis, we constructed a set of FT models which assume that an agent computes the values of action (here, accepting or rejecting) by summing up the current value (CV) and the future value (FV) based on her estimation of the amount of controllability she has over the social interactions.
evidence: This is a description of the computational model.

claim: The forward thinking models incorporate social norm adaptation to characterize how individuals' aversion thresholds to unfairness is adjusted by observing the counterpart teams' proposals.
source: These models also incorporate social norm adaptation (Gu et al., 2015) to characterize how individuals' aversion thresholds to unfairness is adjusted by observing the counterpart teams' proposals (Fehr and Schmidt, 1999) (see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This is a description of the computational model.

claim: The key individual-level parameter-of-interest in the forward thinking model is the 'expected influence,' δ, representing the amount of the offer changes that participants thought they would induce by rejecting the current offer.
source: The key individual-level parameter-of-interest in this model is the 'expected influence,' δ, representing the amount of the offer changes that participants thought they would induce by rejecting the current offer (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a description of the computational model.

claim: For both the Controllable and Uncontrollable conditions, the forward thinking models better explained participants' behavior than the 0-step model.
source: The results showed that for both conditions (Controllable, Uncontrollable), all FT models significantly better explained participants' choices than the standalone norm learning model without FT (0-step model) (Gu et al., 2015), as indexed by Draper's Information Criteria (DIC) (Draper, 1995) scores averaged across individuals (paired t-test comparing 2-step FT model with 0-step model Controllable: t(47)=–4.45, p<0.0001; Uncontrollable: t(47)=–4.21, p<0.001; Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by model comparison using DIC scores and shown in Figure 3b.

claim: All parameters from the forward thinking models were identifiable.
source: In addition, not all parameters were recoverable in parameter recovery analysis using the 0-step model (e.g., sensitivity to norm violation; Controllable: r=–0.03, p=0.82; Uncontrollable: r=0.20, p=0.15) whereas all the parameters from the FT models were identifiable (see Figure 3—figure supplement 3a-j for parameter recovery of the 2-step model).
evidence: This is supported by parameter recovery analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Participants engaged in future-oriented thinking and specifically, calculated how their current choice might affect subsequent social interactions, regardless of the actual level of controllability of the environment.
source: These results suggest that participants engaged in future-oriented thinking and specifically, calculated how their current choice might affect subsequent social interactions, regardless of the actual level of controllability of the environment.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the model comparison results.

claim: The forward thinking models with longer planning horizon tend to show smaller DIC scores (i.e., better model fit), but the fit improvement became marginal after two steps.
source: The FT models with longer planning horizon tend to show smaller DIC scores (i.e., better model fit), but the fit improvement became marginal after two steps (paired t-test comparing 2-step FT model with (i) 1-step Controllable: t(47)=–4.41, p<0.0001, Uncontrollable: t(47)=–3.01, p<0.001; (ii) 3-step Controllable: t(47)=0.39, p=0.70, Uncontrollable: t(47)=–0.04, p=0.97; (iii) 4-step Controllable: t(47)=0.06, p=0.95, Uncontrollable: t(47)=–0.12, p=0.91; Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by model comparison using DIC scores and shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The 2-step forward thinking model predicted participants' choices with an average accuracy rate of 83.7% for the Controllable and 90.1% for the Uncontrollable condition.
source: The 2-step FT model predicted participants' choices with an average accuracy rate of 83.7% for the Controllable and 90.1% for the Uncontrollable condition (Figure 3c), which was higher than the 1-step model for the Controllable condition (Controllable 78.4% (t(47)=–3.63, p<0.001), Uncontrollable 88.7% (t(47)=–1.45, p=0.15)) and comparable with the models with longer planning horizon (3-step model: Controllable 84.0% (t(47)=0.20, p=0.84), Uncontrollable 90.7% (t(47)=0.62, p=0.53); 4-step model: Controllable 84.0% (t(47)=0.21, p=0.84), Uncontrollable 90.2% (t(47)=0.09, p=0.93)).
evidence: This is supported by model prediction accuracy analysis and shown in Figure 3c.

claim: The expected influence parameter estimates drawn from the 2-step forward thinking model were higher for the Controllable than for the Uncontrollable condition.
source: Indeed, we found that the expected influence parameter estimates drawn from the 2-step FT model were higher for the Controllable than for the Uncontrollable condition (meanC=1.33, meanU=0.98, t(47)=2.90, p<0.01; Figure 3d), indicating that participants simulated greater levels of controllability when environments were in fact controllable than when they were uncontrollable.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the model parameters and shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Participants simulated greater levels of controllability when environments were in fact controllable than when they were uncontrollable.
source: Indeed, we found that the expected influence parameter estimates drawn from the 2-step FT model were higher for the Controllable than for the Uncontrollable condition (meanC=1.33, meanU=0.98, t(47)=2.90, p<0.01; Figure 3d), indicating that participants simulated greater levels of controllability when environments were in fact controllable than when they were uncontrollable.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the model parameter estimates.

claim: The expected influence was positively correlated between the conditions.
source: Interestingly, despite the systematic difference between the two conditions, the expected influence was still positively correlated between the conditions (r=0.30, p<0.05; Figure 3e), suggesting a trait-like characteristic of the parameter.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis and shown in Figure 3e.

claim: The expected influence has a trait-like characteristic.
source: Interestingly, despite the systematic difference between the two conditions, the expected influence was still positively correlated between the conditions (r=0.30, p<0.05; Figure 3e), suggesting a trait-like characteristic of the parameter.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation between expected influence in the two conditions.

claim: The self-reported belief about controllability was not correlated between the conditions.
source: This is in contrast with the self-reported belief about controllability, which was not correlated between the conditions (r=–0.18, p=0.26; Figure 3f; correlation between expected influence and self-reported controllability is listed in Figure 4—figure supplement 4a-d).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis and shown in Figure 3f.

claim: There was a positive association between expected influence and task performance during the Controllable condition.
source: Furthermore, we observed a positive association between expected influence and task performance during the Controllable condition (r=0.78, p<<0.0001; Figure 3g).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis and shown in Figure 3g.

claim: Those who simulated a greater level of controllability were able to raise the offers higher, indicating the beneficial effect of doing so.
source: This result suggests that those who simulated a greater level of controllability were able to raise the offers higher, indicating the beneficial effect of doing so.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the positive association between expected influence and task performance.

claim: In the non-social task, participants exhibited similar choice patterns to the social task.
source: Using the same computational models, we found that not only participants exhibited similar choice patterns (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a-c), but also the 2-step FT model was still favored in the non-social task (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d,e) and that delta was still higher for the Controllable than the Uncontrollable condition (Figure 2—figure supplement 1f, meanC=1.31, meanU=0.75, t(26)=2.54, p<0.05).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from the non-social task shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The 2-step forward thinking model was still favored in the non-social task.
source: Using the same computational models, we found that not only participants exhibited similar choice patterns (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a-c), but also the 2-step FT model was still favored in the non-social task (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d,e) and that delta was still higher for the Controllable than the Uncontrollable condition (Figure 2—figure supplement 1f, meanC=1.31, meanU=0.75, t(26)=2.54, p<0.05).
evidence: This is supported by model comparison in the non-social task shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Delta was higher for the Controllable than the Uncontrollable condition in the non-social task.
source: Using the same computational models, we found that not only participants exhibited similar choice patterns (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a-c), but also the 2-step FT model was still favored in the non-social task (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d,e) and that delta was still higher for the Controllable than the Uncontrollable condition (Figure 2—figure supplement 1f, meanC=1.31, meanU=0.75, t(26)=2.54, p<0.05).
evidence: This is supported by model parameter estimates from the non-social task shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Participants' subjective report of controllability did not differentiate between conditions in the non-social task.
source: First, participants' subjective report of controllability did not differentiate between conditions in the non-social task (Figure 2—figure supplement 1g; meanC=62.7, meanU=56.9, t(25)=0.78, p=0.44), which suggests that the social aspect of an environment might have a unique effect on subjective beliefs about controllability.
evidence: This is supported by self-reported controllability data from the non-social task shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1g.

claim: The social aspect of an environment might have a unique effect on subjective beliefs about controllability.
source: First, participants' subjective report of controllability did not differentiate between conditions in the non-social task (Figure 2—figure supplement 1g; meanC=62.7, meanU=56.9, t(25)=0.78, p=0.44), which suggests that the social aspect of an environment might have a unique effect on subjective beliefs about controllability.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the difference in self-reported controllability between the social and non-social tasks.

claim: Despite a similar involvement of forward thinking in exploiting controllability, the social context had a considerable impact on subjective experience during the task.
source: Taken together, these new results suggest that despite of a similar involvement of FT in exploiting controllability, the social context had a considerable impact on subjective experience during the task.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the comparison of social and non-social tasks.

claim: The online sample was more demographically diverse than the fMRI 'healthy' control.
source: Notably, this online sample was more demographically diverse than the fMRI 'healthy' control, because we recruited them without any pre-screening or geographical constraints within the United States.
evidence: This is a description of the online sample.

claim: The offer size increased throughout the trials under the Controllable condition in the online sample.
source: First, we found that the offer size increased throughout the trials under the Controllable condition, replicating the results from the fMRI sample (meanC=6.0, meanU 5.0, t(1,341)=20.29, p<<0.0001; Figure 4a).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from the online sample shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The rejection pattern was different between the two conditions in the online sample, with a more flattened rejection curve for the Controllable than for the Uncontrollable condition.
source: Second, the rejection pattern was different between the two conditions, with a more flattened rejection curve for the Controllable than for the Uncontrollable condition (low ($1–3): meanC=66%, meanU=86%, t(741.54)=–12.28, p<<0.0001; middle ($4–6): meanC=67%, meanU=59%, t(2,606)=5.96, p<<0.0001; high ($7–9): meanC=47%, meanU=15%, t(1,925)=31.67, p<<0.0001; Figure 4b).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from the online sample shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Online participants rejected more medium and high offers under the Controllable than the Uncontrollable, similar to the fMRI participants.
source: Specifically, the online participants rejected more medium and high offers under the Controllable than the Uncontrollable, similar to the fMRI participants.
evidence: This is an observation from the behavioral data of the online sample.

claim: For low offers, online participants showed significantly lower rejection rates under the Controllable than the Uncontrollable condition.
source: Furthermore, for low offers, online participants showed significantly lower rejection rates under the Controllable than the Uncontrollable condition, which trend was not statistically significant for the fMRI sample.
evidence: This is an observation from the behavioral data of the online sample.

claim: Online participants reported higher perceived control for the Controllable than the Uncontrollable as fMRI participants did.
source: Third, online participants reported higher perceived control for the Controllable than the Uncontrollable as fMRI participants did (meanC=58.3, meanU=25.6, t(2,579)=27.93, p<<0.0001; Figure 4c).
evidence: This is supported by self-reported controllability data from the online sample shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The mean of the 2-step forward thinking model's choice prediction accuracy was 80.2% for the Controllable and 93.9% for the Uncontrollable condition in the online sample.
source: First, we assessed the accuracy rate of the 2-step FT model's choice prediction; the mean of which was 80.2% for the Controllable and 93.9% for the Uncontrollable condition (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by model prediction accuracy analysis for the online sample shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The parameters of the 2-step forward thinking model were identifiable for the online sample.
source: The parameters of the 2-step FT model were identifiable for the online sample as well (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b-k).
evidence: This is supported by parameter recovery analysis for the online sample shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The expected influence drawn from the 2-step forward thinking model was higher for the Controllable than the Uncontrollable in the online sample.
source: The expected influence drawn from the 2-step FT model was higher for the Controllable than the Uncontrollable (meanC=1.34, meanU=0.90, t(1,341)=12.97, p<<0.0001; Figure 4d).
evidence: This is supported by model parameter estimates from the online sample shown in Figure 4d.

claim: The expected influence parameters for the two conditions were correlated in the online sample.
source: Yet, consistent with the fMRI sample, the parameters for the two conditions were correlated (r=0.18, p<<0.0001; Figure 4e).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis for the online sample shown in Figure 4e.

claim: The self-reported controllability showed a negative correlation between the conditions in the online sample.
source: The self-reported controllability showed a negative correlation between the conditions (r=–0.10, p<0.001; Figure 4f).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis for the online sample shown in Figure 4f.

claim: The expected influence was positively correlated with the mean offer size in the online sample.
source: In addition, the expected influence was positively correlated with the mean offer size (r=0.50, p<<0.0001; Figure 4g).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis for the online sample shown in Figure 4g.

claim: The independent large-scale replication results show that the suggested future thinking model explains decision processes involved in social controllability of a general population.
source: Taken together, our independent large-scale replication results show that our suggested future thinking model explains decision processes involved in social controllability of a general population.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the online replication study.

claim: A computational model that could explain cognitive processes should not only fit choice behavior well, but also be represented by neurobiological substrates in the brain (i.e., biological plausibility).
source: A computational model that could explain cognitive processes should not only fit choice behavior well, but also be represented by neurobiological substrates in the brain (i.e., biological plausibility) (Cohen et al., 2017; O'Doherty et al., 2007; Wilson and Collins, 2019).
evidence: This is a general principle in computational neuroscience supported by citations.

claim: The total (both current and future) choice values estimated by the 2-step forward thinking model, but not those from the 0-step model (only CVs), would be signaled in the vmPFC.
source: Accordingly, we expected that the total (both current and future) choice values estimated by the 2-step FT model, but not those from the 0-step model (only CVs), would be signaled in the vmPFC, a brain region that is known to process subjective values (Bartra et al., 2013; Hiser and Koenigs, 2018) during both social and non-social decision-making.
evidence: This is a prediction based on prior research on the vmPFC.

claim: The BOLD signals in the vmPFC tracked the value estimates drawn from the 2-step planning model across both conditions.
source: These analyses showed that the BOLD signals in the vmPFC tracked the value estimates drawn from the 2-step planning model across both conditions (PFDR<0.05, k>50; Figure 5a, Supplementary file 1e), and there was no significant difference between the two conditions (PFDR<0.05).
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data shown in Figure 5a and Supplementary file 1e.

claim: There was no significant difference in vmPFC BOLD responses between the two conditions.
source: These analyses showed that the BOLD signals in the vmPFC tracked the value estimates drawn from the 2-step planning model across both conditions (PFDR<0.05, k>50; Figure 5a, Supplementary file 1e), and there was no significant difference between the two conditions (PFDR<0.05).
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data.

claim: BOLD responses in the vmPFC did not track the trial-by-trial value estimates from the 0-step model, even at a more liberal threshold.
source: In contrast, BOLD responses in the vmPFC did not track the trial-by-trial value estimates from the 0-step model, even at a more liberal threshold (p<0.005 uncorrected, k>50; Figure 5b, Supplementary file 1f).
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data shown in Figure 5b and Supplementary file 1f.

claim: The vmPFC encoded total values rather than only current value or future value.
source: We also conducted model comparison at the neural level using the MACS toolbox (see Figure 5—figure supplement 3 for details) and found that the vmPFC encoded TVs rather than only CV or FV.
evidence: This is supported by neural model comparison shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: The vmPFC ROI coefficients for the 2-step forward thinking's value estimates were significantly greater than 0 for both the Controllable and Uncontrollable conditions.
source: This analysis showed that the vmPFC ROI coefficients for the choice values were significantly greater for the 2-step model than for the 0-step model regardless of the condition (Controllable: t(46)=1.81, p<0.05 (one-tailed); Uncontrollable: t(46)=2.04, p<0.05 (one-tailed); Figure 5c). Indeed, the ROI coefficients based on the 2-step model were significantly larger than zero for each condition (Controllable: meanC=0.29, t(47)=1.96, p<0.05 (one-tailed); Uncontrollable: meanU=0.24, t(47)=2.14, p<0.05 (one-tailed); Figure 5c) whereas these coefficients for the choice values (CV only) based on the 0-step model were not significant for either condition (Controllable: meanC=0.09, t(46)=0.69, p=0.25 (one-tailed); Uncontrollable: meanU=0.12, t(46)=1.17, p=0.12 (one-tailed); Figure 5c).
evidence: This is supported by ROI analysis shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The ROI coefficients based on the 2-step model were significantly larger than zero for each condition.
source: Indeed, the ROI coefficients based on the 2-step model were significantly larger than zero for each condition (Controllable: meanC=0.29, t(47)=1.96, p<0.05 (one-tailed); Uncontrollable: meanU=0.24, t(47)=2.14, p<0.05 (one-tailed); Figure 5c) whereas these coefficients for the choice values (CV only) based on the 0-step model were not significant for either condition (Controllable: meanC=0.09, t(46)=0.69, p=0.25 (one-tailed); Uncontrollable: meanU=0.12, t(46)=1.17, p=0.12 (one-tailed); Figure 5c).
evidence: This is supported by ROI analysis shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The coefficients for the choice values (CV only) based on the 0-step model were not significant for either condition.
source: Indeed, the ROI coefficients based on the 2-step model were significantly larger than zero for each condition (Controllable: meanC=0.29, t(47)=1.96, p<0.05 (one-tailed); Uncontrollable: meanU=0.24, t(47)=2.14, p<0.05 (one-tailed); Figure 5c) whereas these coefficients for the choice values (CV only) based on the 0-step model were not significant for either condition (Controllable: meanC=0.09, t(46)=0.69, p=0.25 (one-tailed); Uncontrollable: meanU=0.12, t(46)=1.17, p=0.12 (one-tailed); Figure 5c).
evidence: This is supported by ROI analysis shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Individuals engaged the vmPFC to compute the projected total (current and future) values of their choices during forward thinking.
source: These findings suggest that individuals engaged the vmPFC to compute the projected total (current and future) values of their choices during FT.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the fMRI results.

claim: vmPFC signals were comparable between the two conditions both in the whole-brain analysis and the ROI analyses.
source: Furthermore, vmPFC signals were comparable between the two conditions both in the whole-brain analysis and the ROI analyses.
evidence: This is an observation from the fMRI results.

claim: Humans computed summed choice values regardless of the actual controllability of the social environment.
source: Consistent with our behavioral modeling results, these neural results further support the notion that humans computed summed choice values regardless of the actual controllability of the social environment.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the fMRI results.

claim: Norm prediction errors were encoded in the ventral striatum (VS) and the right anterior insula (rAI) for the Controllable condition.
source: We found that nPEs were encoded in the ventral striatum (VS; [4, 14, −14]) and the right anterior insula (rAI; [32, 16, −14]) for the Controllable condition (Figure 5—figure supplement 4a), while these signals were found in the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC; [2, 46, 16]) for the Uncontrollable condition (Figure 5—figure supplement 4b) at PFWE <0.05, small volume corrected.
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4a.

claim: Norm prediction error signals were found in the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) for the Uncontrollable condition.
source: We found that nPEs were encoded in the ventral striatum (VS; [4, 14, −14]) and the right anterior insula (rAI; [32, 16, −14]) for the Controllable condition (Figure 5—figure supplement 4a), while these signals were found in the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC; [2, 46, 16]) for the Uncontrollable condition (Figure 5—figure supplement 4b) at PFWE <0.05, small volume corrected.
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4b.

claim: The VS and the rAI had significantly greater BOLD responses for the Controllable than the Uncontrollable condition.
source: We further contrasted the whole-brain map of the two conditions and found that the VS ([4, 14, −14]) and the rAI ([32, 16, −14]) had significantly greater BOLD responses for the Controllable than the Uncontrollable condition (PFWE<0.05, small volume corrected; Figure 5—figure supplement 4c) whereas the ACC ([2, 46, 16]) response under the Uncontrollable condition was not significantly greater than the Controllable condition at the same threshold (Figure 5—figure supplement 4d).
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4c.

claim: The ACC response under the Uncontrollable condition was not significantly greater than the Controllable condition.
source: We further contrasted the whole-brain map of the two conditions and found that the VS ([4, 14, −14]) and the rAI ([32, 16, −14]) had significantly greater BOLD responses for the Controllable than the Uncontrollable condition (PFWE<0.05, small volume corrected; Figure 5—figure supplement 4c) whereas the ACC ([2, 46, 16]) response under the Uncontrollable condition was not significantly greater than the Controllable condition at the same threshold (Figure 5—figure supplement 4d).
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4d.

claim: Internal norm-related BOLD signals were tracked in the VS for the Controllable condition.
source: We also found that internal norm-related BOLD signals were tracked in the VS ([10, 16, −2]) for the Controllable condition (Figure 5—figure supplement 4a), and in the rAI ([28, 16, −6]) and the amygdala ([18, −6, −8]) for the Uncontrollable condition (Figure 5—figure supplement 5b) at PFWE<0.05, small volume corrected.
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5a.

claim: Internal norm-related BOLD signals were tracked in the rAI and the amygdala for the Uncontrollable condition.
source: We also found that internal norm-related BOLD signals were tracked in the VS ([10, 16, −2]) for the Controllable condition (Figure 5—figure supplement 4a), and in the rAI ([28, 16, −6]) and the amygdala ([18, −6, −8]) for the Uncontrollable condition (Figure 5—figure supplement 5b) at PFWE<0.05, small volume corrected.
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5b.

claim: The difference in internal norm-related BOLD signals between the conditions was not statistically significant in the whole-brain contrast.
source: However, the difference between the conditions was not statistically significant in the whole-brain contrast (Figure 5—figure supplement 5c-d).
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5c-d.

claim: The controllability level of the social interaction modulates neural encoding of internal norm representation and adaptation.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that the controllability level of the social interaction modulates neural encoding of internal norm representation and adaptation, expanding our previous knowledge about the computational mechanisms of norm learning (Gu et al., 2015; Xiang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the fMRI results on norm prediction errors and norm estimates.

claim: vmPFC signal was positively correlated with the disconnection between self-reported controllability and expected influence in the uncontrollable environment.
source: Specifically, vmPFC signals were positively correlated with the disconnection between self-reported controllability and expected influence in the uncontrollable environment (r=0.35, p<0.05; Figure 5—figure supplement 1a), but not in the controllable environment (r=–0.14, p=0.38; Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1a.

claim: vmPFC signals were not correlated with the disconnection between self-reported controllability and expected influence in the controllable environment.
source: Specifically, vmPFC signals were positively correlated with the disconnection between self-reported controllability and expected influence in the uncontrollable environment (r=0.35, p<0.05; Figure 5—figure supplement 1a), but not in the controllable environment (r=–0.14, p=0.38; Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The meaning of vmPFC encoding of value signals could be context-dependent.
source: These results suggest that the meaning of vmPFC encoding of value signals could be context-dependent—and that heightened vmPFC signaling in uncontrollable situations is related to overly optimistic beliefs about controllability.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation between vmPFC signals and belief-behavior disconnection.

claim: Heightened vmPFC signaling in uncontrollable situations is related to overly optimistic beliefs about controllability.
source: These results suggest that the meaning of vmPFC encoding of value signals could be context-dependent—and that heightened vmPFC signaling in uncontrollable situations is related to overly optimistic beliefs about controllability.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation between vmPFC signals and belief-behavior disconnection.

claim: For social animals like humans, it is crucial to be able to exploit the controllability of our social interactions and to consider the long-term social effects of our current choices.
source: For social animals like humans, it is crucial to be able to exploit the controllability of our social interactions and to consider the long-term social effects of our current choices.
evidence: This is a general statement in the discussion.

claim: This study provides a mechanistic account for how humans identify and use social controllability.
source: This study provides a mechanistic account for how humans identify and use social controllability.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's contribution.

claim: Humans are capable of exploiting the controllability of their social interactions and exert influence on social others when given the opportunity.
source: In two independent samples of human participants, we demonstrate that (1) humans are capable of exploiting the controllability of their social interactions and exert influence on social others when given the opportunity, and that (2) they do so by engaging a mental model of FT and calculating the downstream effects of their current social choices.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: Humans exploit social controllability by engaging a mental model of forward thinking and calculating the downstream effects of their current social choices.
source: In two independent samples of human participants, we demonstrate that (1) humans are capable of exploiting the controllability of their social interactions and exert influence on social others when given the opportunity, and that (2) they do so by engaging a mental model of FT and calculating the downstream effects of their current social choices.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: The vmPFC represents combined signals of current value and future value during forward social planning.
source: By using model-based fMRI analytic approach, we demonstrate that the vmPFC represents combined signals of CV and FV during forward social planning; and that this neural value representation was positively associated with belief-behavior disconnect in the Uncontrollable condition.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: The neural value representation in the vmPFC was positively associated with belief-behavior disconnect in the Uncontrollable condition.
source: By using model-based fMRI analytic approach, we demonstrate that the vmPFC represents combined signals of CV and FV during forward social planning; and that this neural value representation was positively associated with belief-behavior disconnect in the Uncontrollable condition.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: People use vmPFC-dependent forward thinking to guide social choices, expanding the role of this neurocomputational mechanism beyond subjective valuation.
source: These findings demonstrate that people use vmPFC-dependent FT to guide social choices, expanding the role of this neurocomputational mechanism beyond subjective valuation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study.

claim: Forward thinking is an important high-level cognitive process that is frequently associated with abstract reasoning, planning, and model-based control.
source: FT is an important high-level cognitive process that is frequently associated with abstract reasoning (Hegarty, 2004), planning (Szpunar et al., 2014), and model-based control (Constantinescu et al., 2016; Daw et al., 2011; Gläscher et al., 2010; Schuck et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Forward thinking has been suggested to involve four intertwined modes: mental simulation, prediction, intention, and planning.
source: Also known as prospection, FT has been suggested to involve four intertwined modes: mental simulation, prediction, intention, and planning (Szpunar et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: All four modes of forward thinking (mental simulation, prediction, intention, and planning) are likely to have taken place in the current study.
source: All four modes are likely to have taken place in our study, as our FT model implies that a social decision-maker mentally simulates social value functions into the future, predicts how her action would affect the following offers from partners, sets a goal of increasing future offers, and plans steps ahead to achieve the goal.
evidence: This is an inference about the cognitive processes involved in the task.

claim: Humans can learn and strategically exploit controllability during various forms of exchanges with others.
source: Critically relevant to the current study, previous research suggests that humans can learn and strategically exploit controllability during various forms of exchanges with others (Bhatt et al., 2010; Camerer, 2011; Hampton et al., 2008; Hula et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The current study shows that humans can also exploit controllability and exert their influence even when interacting with a series of other players.
source: Here, we show that humans can also exploit controllability and exert their influence even when interacting with a series of other players (as opposed to a single other player as tested in previous studies).
evidence: This is a summary of a key contribution of the current study.

claim: The 2-step forward thinking model captures the explicit magnitude of controllability in individuals' mental models of an environment.
source: Furthermore, our 2-step FT model captures the explicit magnitude of controllability in individuals' mental models of an environment, which can be intuitively compared to subjective, psychological controllability.
evidence: This is a description of a key feature of the computational model.

claim: The 2-step forward thinking model simultaneously incorporates aversion to norm violation and norm adaptation, two important parameters guiding social adaptation.
source: Finally, our 2-step FT model simultaneously incorporates aversion to norm violation and norm adaptation, two important parameters guiding social adaptation (Fehr, 2004; Gu et al., 2015; Spitzer et al., 2007; Zhang and Gläscher, 2020).
evidence: This is a description of a key feature of the computational model.

claim: Individuals who showed higher expected influence performed better in terms of achieving higher offers from their partners under the Controllable condition.
source: We found that individuals who showed higher δ performed better in terms of achieving higher offers from their partners under the Controllable condition, suggesting a direct association between FT and performance in strategic social interaction.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis between expected influence and task performance.

claim: There is a direct association between forward thinking and performance in strategic social interaction.
source: We found that individuals who showed higher δ performed better in terms of achieving higher offers from their partners under the Controllable condition, suggesting a direct association between FT and performance in strategic social interaction.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation between expected influence and task performance.

claim: People's behavior was better explained by the 2-step forward thinking model than the 0-step no planning model even for the Uncontrollable condition.
source: Although δ was higher in the Controllable than the Uncontrollable condition, one surprising finding is that people's behavior was better explained by the 2-step FT model than the 0-step no planning model even for the Uncontrollable condition.
evidence: This is an observation from the model comparison results.

claim: Participants still expected some level of influence (controllability) over their partners' offers even when environment was in fact uncontrollable.
source: These results suggest that participants still expected some level of influence (controllability) over their partners' offers even when environment was in fact uncontrollable.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the model comparison results.

claim: People still attempted to simulate future interactions in uncontrollable situations due to their preference and tendency to control.
source: We speculate that people still attempted to simulate future interactions in uncontrollable situations due to their preference and tendency to control (Leotti and Delgado, 2014; Shenhav et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculation about why people engaged forward thinking in the Uncontrollable condition.

claim: There are currently at least two distinct views about the role of the vmPFC.
source: There are currently at least two distinct views about the role of the vmPFC.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The first view considers the vmPFC to encode a generic value signal (e.g., the common currency), including the value of social information and anticipatory utility.
source: The first view considers the vmPFC to encode a generic value signal (e.g., the common currency; Levy and Glimcher, 2012), including the value of social information (Behrens et al., 2008; Chung et al., 2015) and anticipatory utility (Iigaya et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: An alternative theory suggests that the vmPFC represents mental maps of state space and of conceptual knowledge.
source: An alternative theory suggests that the vmPFC represents mental maps of state space (Schuck et al., 2016) and of conceptual knowledge (Constantinescu et al., 2016), in addition to other 'map'-encoding brain structures such as the hippocampus (O'keefe and Nadel, 1978; Tavares et al., 2015) and entorhinal cortex (Stensola et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The exact function of the vmPFC could depend on the specific setup of the task environment.
source: Of course, these views of the vmPFC might not necessarily be in contradiction. Instead, the exact function of the vmPFC could depend on the specific setup of the task environment.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential reconciliation of different views on vmPFC function.

claim: In the current task, the vmPFC computed a summed value of not only the current state, but also future states.
source: In the particular case of our task, as explicit values are inherently embedded in each state (i.e., each interaction), the vmPFC computed a summed value of not only the current state, but also future states.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the fMRI results in the context of the task.

claim: Both types of computations (value encoding and map representation) could be required to calculate the total downstream values of current social choices in the current experimental setup.
source: That is, both types of computations could be required to calculate the total downstream values of current social choices in our experimental setup.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the fMRI results in the context of the task.

claim: vmPFC signal was amplified by illusory beliefs only when the social environment was uncontrollable (but not when environment was controllable).
source: We also found that vmPFC signal was amplified by illusory beliefs only when the social environment was uncontrollable (but not when environment was controllable), suggesting that the behavioral relevance of value-encoding in the vmPFC is context-dependent.
evidence: This is an observation from the exploratory fMRI analysis.

claim: The behavioral relevance of value-encoding in the vmPFC is context-dependent.
source: We also found that vmPFC signal was amplified by illusory beliefs only when the social environment was uncontrollable (but not when environment was controllable), suggesting that the behavioral relevance of value-encoding in the vmPFC is context-dependent.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the exploratory fMRI analysis.

claim: The neural results illustrate a role of the vmPFC in constructing the total values (both current value and future value) of current actions as humans engaged in forward planning during social exchange.
source: Taken together, our neural results illustrate a role of the vmPFC in constructing the TVs (both CV and FV) of current actions as humans engaged in forward planning during social exchange; and that these vmPFC-encoded values signals can be counterproductive and relate to exaggerated illusory beliefs about controllability when environment does not allow control.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the fMRI results.

claim: vmPFC-encoded values signals can be counterproductive and relate to exaggerated illusory beliefs about controllability when environment does not allow control.
source: Taken together, our neural results illustrate a role of the vmPFC in constructing the TVs (both CV and FV) of current actions as humans engaged in forward planning during social exchange; and that these vmPFC-encoded values signals can be counterproductive and relate to exaggerated illusory beliefs about controllability when environment does not allow control.

claim: The proposed model showcases how forward thinking can help optimize normative social behavior, as often required during strategic social interaction.
